consensus_summary: Mercy is God's compassionate disposition toward sinners and sufferers—His withholding of deserved judgment and His active lovingkindness—supremely expressed in Christ, with human mercy as derivative imitation. Covenant loyalty (hesed), the mercy seat typology, and ethical works of mercy are all recognized as common facets, but the primary identification is divine compassionate non-retribution, typically distinguished from grace as sparing merited punishment versus giving unmerited favor.
book_summary: Mercy is covenant loyalty expressed through compassion, forgiveness, and faithful dealing. It carries built-in obligations: mercy received obligates the recipient to show mercy (Matt 18:27-35; 5:7), and pardon is joined with confession and forsaking of sin (Prov 28:13). The book explicitly notes the common teaching—compassion withholding deserved punishment—is usually summarized without these covenant obligations.
consensus_core_identification: Divine compassionate withholding of deserved judgment plus active lovingkindness toward the guilty and needy, imitated derivatively by believers.
book_core_identification: Covenant loyalty (hesed) manifested as compassion and forgiveness, structurally conditioned by covenant obligations: confession/forsaking as the condition of receiving pardon, and reciprocal mercy as the obligation of having received it.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus treats mercy first as unconditional compassionate non-retribution, with covenant loyalty and human obligation as secondary facets or alternatives. The book promotes the hesed/covenant framing to the core and attaches conditions the consensus summary leaves out: mercy without confession and forsaking (Prov 28:13) is not obtained, and mercy received without reciprocal mercy shown is forfeited (Matt 18:32-35). Cases of mercy conceived as bare leniency detached from covenant obligations are excluded or reclassified by the book.
rationale: The book's central referent—God's compassionate forgiveness toward people—remains the same as the consensus's, and its covenant-loyalty framing is explicitly listed as a common alternative in every consensus response (hesed). What the book changes materially is the boundary and conditions: it insists mercy is inseparable from covenant structure, joining pardon to confession/forsaking and making received mercy generate an enforceable obligation to show mercy. The book's own common-view note confirms it is correcting an omission ('often summarized without the covenant obligations surrounding it') rather than replacing the referent. This is genuine boundary disagreement within the same category, fitting REFINED, not DIVERGENT—both readings can be true of the same referent, with the book conditioning what the consensus leaves unconditional.
strongest_objection: One could argue this is merely a MATCH: covenant loyalty (hesed) and the obligation of human mercy (Matt 18; Matt 5:7; James 2:13) are already present as common facets in every consensus response, so the book may only be re-weighting emphases rather than materially changing the extension. However, the book's insistence that pardon is conditioned on confession/forsaking and that mercy received creates a binding, forfeitable obligation goes beyond the consensus's unconditional-compassion framing, which the book itself flags as incomplete.
